lead: An electronic engine control unit (ECU) is a small computer that runs the engine. It reads sensors, looks up calibrated tables called maps, and drives injectors, the ignition coil and valves in a repeating loop. It exists because a three-way catalyst needs the air-fuel ratio held within about one percent of λ = 1 for a whole vehicle life, through wear, heat and altitude. No carburettor or mechanical distributor can do that. Petrol engines use this stoichiometric loop. Diesel engines also have an ECU, but they always run lean (λ well above 1) and control injected fuel quantity directly, cleaning the exhaust with an oxidation catalyst, a particulate filter and selective catalytic reduction instead of a three-way catalyst.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the legal limit, 4.2 for the air-fuel compromise, and 4.3 for the targets the maps hold.

sections.h3: Why a computer, and what a loop means

blocks.text: Petrol burns cleanly in a three-way catalyst only when the exhaust stays within a narrow band around λ = 1. Here λ (the excess-air ratio) = actual air-fuel ratio ÷ stoichiometric air-fuel ratio. λ = 1 means the mixture is exactly stoichiometric; λ = 1.05 means 5 percent more air than stoichiometric. The catalyst converts carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides at once in that band; outside it, conversion of at least one pollutant collapses. The band is about one percent wide in λ. A carburettor meters fuel through fixed jets and a venturi. Its mixture drifts with jet wear, fuel pressure, air density, altitude and engine temperature. It cannot hold one percent over ten years and 150 000 km. The electronic control unit (ECU) can, because it measures and corrects.

Open loop means the ECU computes an output from stored calibration alone. It looks up a number and fires the injector for that long, with no sensor confirming the result. The assumption is that fuel pressure, airflow and injector flow are exactly as calibrated.

Closed loop means a sensor measures the result and the ECU corrects the output. The exhaust oxygen (lambda) sensor produces a voltage that switches sharply from lean to rich at λ = 1. A zirconia switching sensor gives about 0.1 V when the exhaust is lean and about 0.8 to 0.9 V when rich, crossing over within a very small change of λ around 1; the ECU treats roughly 0.45 V as the switch point. The ECU compares the measured mixture with its target and adds a correction, called a trim. Electronic hardware alone does not make a loop; a table lookup is still open loop until a measurement closes it.

sections.h3: Inside the ECU: signals, maps and interpolation

blocks.text: Signal path. A sensor output is rarely ready for a processor. Signal conditioning scales it into the analogue-to-digital converter's (ADC) input range, filters radio-frequency noise, and protects against voltage spikes. The ADC turns the voltage into a count. A 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference gives 2¹⁰ = 1024 steps, so one count is 5 ÷ 1024 ≈ 4.9 mV.

The processor runs a program stored in flash memory, uses RAM for temporary values, and keeps adaptive trims in non-volatile memory (EEPROM or flash) in most modern ECUs; older designs hold them in keep-alive RAM, which loses the learned trims when the battery is disconnected. Driver stages are power switches, usually low-side n-channel MOSFETs that ground one end of an injector or coil; a flyback diode catches the inductive kick when the switch opens.

Calibration grid. The central object is a two-dimensional table, also called a map. One axis is engine speed in rpm, the other is load — manifold absolute pressure (MAP) in kPa, or air mass per stroke in mg. Each cell stores one calibrated value: injector open time, spark advance, idle valve position, EGR lift, target lambda. Values come from bench and vehicle tests, not from a formula.

blocks.where: y is the value wanted (for example injector open time in ms); x is the measured speed or load; (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) are the two neighbouring calibrated cells.

blocks.text: At a speed and load between cells, the ECU interpolates linearly along each axis. The full set of cells is the engine map. A three-dimensional surface uses the same idea with four surrounding cells.

blocks.text: Air measurement. The ECU must know the trapped air mass to compute fuel. Two methods are common. Speed density computes air from MAP, intake air temperature and volumetric efficiency, which is itself a map. Mass airflow measures it directly with a hot-film or hot-wire sensor in the intake. Chapter 4.5 computes the injection time from either method.

figure.caption: The ECU runs a loop: sensors are conditioned and digitised, maps decide the outputs, and the lambda sensor feeds the result back so the mixture can be trimmed.

spec.title: Engine management loop
spec.aria: Sensors such as manifold pressure, throttle, coolant and lambda feed conditioning circuits, the ECU looks up its maps and drives injectors, the coil and the EGR valve, and the lambda sensor feeds the result back.

examples.question: In the injection-duration map for a warm engine, the column for 2000 rpm holds 4.0 ms at 40 kPa manifold pressure and 6.0 ms at 50 kPa. The ECU reads 46 kPa. Find the injector pulse width, and the fraction of one engine cycle it takes.
steps: The measured load 46 kPa lies between the calibrated cells 40 kPa and 50 kPa at 2000 rpm, so interpolate along the load axis.
A four-stroke cycle takes two revolutions. One revolution takes 60 ÷ 2000 s = 0.030 s, so one cycle is 0.060 s = 60 ms.
Fraction of cycle = 5.2 ÷ 60 = 0.0867, which is 8.7 percent.
examples.answer: The injector is open for 5.2 ms, which is 8.7 percent of the 60 ms four-stroke cycle.
examples.check:
pw = 4.0 + (6.0 - 4.0) * (46 - 40) / (50 - 40)
cycle_ms = 2 * 60 / 2000 * 1000
frac_pct = pw / cycle_ms * 100
print(f"{pw:.1f}")
print(f"{cycle_ms:.1f}")
print(f"{frac_pct:.1f}")

traps: Calling a map-based output 'closed loop'. A lookup from a table is open loop even though it is electronic; the loop closes only when a sensor measures the result and the ECU corrects for it.
Interpolating along the wrong axis. The rpm column and the load row are different axes; use the two cells that bracket the measured load at the same speed.
Mixing milliseconds and percent. Pulse width is an open time in ms; duty is that time divided by the cycle time, and a four-stroke cycle is two revolutions, not one.
Treating λ = 1 as the target everywhere. At full load the ECU deliberately runs rich in open loop to protect exhaust valves, and during cranking and warm-up the lambda sensor is not used.
Thinking limp-home is normal closed loop. Limp-home replaces a failed sensor with a fixed substitute value and limits engine output; it keeps the car moving, not emissions compliant.

quiz.q: Define open-loop and closed-loop engine control in one sentence each.
quiz.a: Open loop computes the output from stored maps alone, with no measurement of the result. Closed loop measures the result with a sensor and corrects the output to reach the target.

quiz.q: List the signal path from a sensor to an actuator in an engine management system.
quiz.a: Sensor → signal conditioning (filter and scale) → analogue-to-digital converter → processor with memory → driver stage → actuator.

quiz.q: Why does a three-way catalyst force the ECU to hold λ within about one percent?
quiz.a: The catalyst converts CO, HC and NOx together only in a narrow band around λ = 1. If the mixture drifts rich, CO and HC conversion falls; if it drifts lean, NOx conversion falls. One percent is the practical width of that window over the life of the vehicle.

quiz.q: A warm-engine injection map at 3000 rpm stores 3.5 ms at 30 kPa and 5.5 ms at 40 kPa. The ECU reads 36 kPa. Find the pulse width and the percentage of one four-stroke cycle.
The lambda sensor fails on a highway cruise. What does the ECU do, and which control mode is active?
quiz.a: The ECU detects the missing or stuck sensor signal and enters limp-home. It discards closed-loop trim, substitutes a fixed or mapped pulse width, and may limit rpm. The engine runs open loop with poorer emission control but keeps the vehicle moving.

quiz.q: An injector is open for 6 ms in a four-stroke cycle at 2500 rpm. Find the cycle time and the duty percentage.
Why does the ECU need two different ways to measure air, speed density and mass airflow?
quiz.a: Speed density is cheap and robust because it uses MAP and a volumetric-efficiency map, but it is sensitive to camshaft changes and altitude unless calibrated. Mass airflow measures air directly and handles those changes, but the hot-film sensor is costlier and can be contaminated. Manufacturers choose by engine type, cost and required accuracy.

quiz.q: What is deceleration fuel cut and why does it save fuel and emissions?
quiz.a: When the throttle is closed and engine speed is above about 1500 rpm, the ECU switches the injectors off. The engine is driven by the wheels, so no fuel is needed. Fuel and emissions fall to zero during the cut; injection resumes near idle to prevent a stall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ECUs are calibrated with model-based methods and hardware-in-the-loop rigs, where an engine model runs in real time and the ECU drives it. Torque structure splits one driver demand into airflow, fuel and spark paths. Cylinder pressure sensors and ion-current sensing are being researched for closed-loop combustion control. Search for "model-based calibration", "hardware-in-the-loop engine" and "torque structure ECU".
